entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 4 1Ti 4:1-16 . Prediction of a Coming Departure from the Faith: Timothy's Duty as to It: General Directions to Him. The "mystery of iniquity" here alluded to, and already working ( 2Th 2:7 ), stands opposed to the "mystery of godliness" just mentioned ( 1Ti 3:16 ). 1. Now-- Greek, "But." In contrast to the "mystery of godliness." the Spirit-- speaking by the prophets in the Church (whose prophecies rested on those of the Old Testament, Da 7:25 ; 8:23 , &c.; 11:30, as also on those of Jesus in the New Testament, Mt 24:11-24 ), and also by Paul himself, 2Th 2:3 (with whom accord 2Pe 3:3 ; 1Jo 2:18 ; Jude 18). expressly-- "in plain words." This shows that he refers to prophecies of the Spirit then lying before him. in the latter times-- in the times following upon the times in which he is now writing. Not some remote future, but times immediately subsequent, the beginnings of the apostasy being already discernible ( Ac 20:29 ): these are the forerunners of "the last days" ( 2Ti 3:1 ). depart from the faith-- The apostasy was to be within the Church, the faithful one becoming the harlot. In 2Th 2:3 (written earlier), the apostasy of the Jews from God (joining the heathen against Christianity) is the groundwork on which the prophecy rises; whereas here, in the Pastoral Epistles, the prophecy is connected with Gnostic errors, the seeds of which had already been sown in the Church [Auberlen] ( 2Ti 2:18 ). Apollonius Tyanæus, a heretic, came to Ephesus in the lifetime of Timothy. giving heed-- ( 1Ti 1:4 ; Tit 1:14 ). seducing spirits-- working in the heretical teachers. 1Jo 4:2 , 3, 6 , "the spirit of error," opposed to "the spirit of truth," "the Spirit" which "speaketh" in the true prophets against them. doctrines of devils-- literally "teachings of (that is suggested by) demons." Jas 3:15 , "wisdom ... devilish"; 2Co 11:15 , "Satan's ministers."

Rather translate, "Through (literally, 'in'; the element in which the apostasy has place) the hypocrisy of lying speakers"; this expresses the means through which "some shall (be led to) depart from the faith," namely, the reigned sanctity of the seducers (compare "deceivers," <reference osisRef="Titus.1.10">Tit 1:10</reference>).<div eID="gen37283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37284" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having their conscience seared--</hi>Greek, "having their own conscience," &c., that is, not only "speaking lies" to others, but also having their own conscience seared. Professing to lead others to holiness, their own conscience is all the while defiled. Bad consciences always have recourse to hypocrisy. As faith and a good conscience are joined (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1Ti 1:5</reference>); so hypocrisy (that is, unbelief, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.5">Mt 24:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.51">51</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Luke.12.46">Lu 12:46</reference>) and a bad conscience here. Theodoret explains like English Version, "seared," as implying their extreme insensibility; the effect of cauterizing being to deaden sensation. The Greek, however, primarily means "branded" with the consciousness of crimes committed against their better knowledge and conscience, like so many scars burnt in by a branding iron: Compare <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">3:11</reference>, "condemned of himself." They are conscious of the brand within, and yet with a hypocritical show of sanctity, they strive to seduce others. As "a seal" is used in a good sense (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference>), so "a brand" in a bad sense. The image is taken from the branding of criminals. <div eID="gen37284" type="x-p"/>

Sensuality leads to false spiritualism. Their own inward impurity is reflected in their eyes in the world without them, and hence their asceticism (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.14">Tit 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.15">15</reference>) [Wiesinger]. By a spurious spiritualism (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>), which made moral perfection consist in abstinence from outward things, they pretended to attain to a higher perfection. <reference osisRef="Matt.19.10-Matt.19.12">Mt 19:10-12</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.8">1Co 7:8</reference>, 26, 38) gave a seeming handle to their "forbidding marriage" (contrast <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.14">1Ti 5:14</reference>); and the Old Testament distinction as to clean and unclean, gave a pretext for teaching to "abstain from meats" (compare <reference osisRef="Col.2.16">Col 2:16</reference>, 17, 20-23). As these Judaizing Gnostics combined the harlot or apostate Old Testament Church with the beast (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.3">Re 17:3</reference>), or Gnostic spiritualizing anti-Christianity, so Rome's Judaizing elements (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:3</reference>) shall ultimately be combined with the open worldly-wise anti-Christianity of the false prophet or beast (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">1Ti 6:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.8">Col 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.1-1John.4.3">1Jo 4:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.12-Rev.13.15">Re 13:12-15</reference>). Austerity gained for them a show of sanctity while preaching false doctrine (<reference osisRef="Col.2.23">Col 2:23</reference>). Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 4.29] quotes from Irenæus [1.28] a statement that Saturninus, Marcion, and the Encratites preached abstinence from marriage and animal meats. Paul prophetically warns against such notions, the seeds of which already were being sown (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">1Ti 6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.17">2Ti 2:17</reference>, 18).<div eID="gen37285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37286" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be received--</hi>Greek, "to be partaken of."<div eID="gen37286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37287" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of them--</hi>literally, (created and designed) "for them," Though all (even the unbelieving, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.14">Psa 104:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">Mt 5:45</reference>) are partakers in these foods created by God, "they which believe" alone fulfil God's design in creation by partaking of them with thanksgiving; as opposed to those who abstain from them, or in partaking of them, do not do so with thanksgiving. The unbelieving have not the designed use of such foods by reason of their "conscience being defiled" (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>). The children of God alone "inherit the earth"; for obedience is the necessary qualification (as it was in the original grant of the earth to Adam), which they alone possess.<div eID="gen37287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37288" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and know the truth--</hi>explanatory and defining who are "they which believe." Translate as Greek, "and have full knowledge of the truth" (see on <reference osisRef="Phil.1.9">Php 1:9</reference>). Thus he contradicts the assumption of superior knowledge and higher moral perfection, put forward by the heretics, on the ground of their abstinence from marriage and meats. "The truth" stands in opposition to their "lies" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.2">1Ti 4:2</reference>). <div eID="gen37288" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18114"/><div sID="gen37304" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18114"/><hi type="bold">8. profiteth little--</hi>Greek, "profiteth to (but) a small extent." Paul does not deny that fasting and abstinence from conjugal intercourse for a time, with a view to reaching the inward man through the outward, do profit somewhat, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.3">Ac 13:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.5">1Co 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.26">9:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.27">27</reference> (though in its degenerate form, asceticism, dwelling solely on what is outward, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:3</reference>, is not only not profitable but injurious). Timothy seems to have had a leaning to such outward self-discipline (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.23">1Ti 5:23</reference>). Paul, therefore, while not disapproving of this in its due proportion and place, shows the vast superiority of godliness or piety, as being profitable not merely "to a small extent," but unto all things; for, having its seat within, it extends thence to the whole outward life of a man. Not unto one portion only of his being, but to every portion of it, bodily and spiritual, temporal and eternal [Alford]. "He who has piety (which is 'profitable unto all things') wants nothing needed to his well-being, even though he be without those helps which, 'to a small extent,' bodily exercise furnishes" [Calvin]. "Life" in its truest and best sense now and hereafter (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.1">2Ti 1:1</reference>). Length of life now so far as it is really good for the believer; life in its truest enjoyments and employments now, and life blessed and eternal hereafter (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.33">Mt 6:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.10.29">Mr 10:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.10.30">30</reference>). Compare Solomon's prayer and the answer (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.7-1Kgs.3.13">1Ki 3:7-13</reference>). <div eID="gen37305" type="x-p"/>

In <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2Ti 1:6</reference> the gift is represented as a spark of the Spirit lying within him, and sure to smoulder by neglect, the stirring up or keeping in lively exercise of which depends on the will of him on whom it is bestowed (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.18">Mt 25:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.27">25, 27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.28">28</reference>). "By" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2Ti 1:6</reference>) implies that Paul's laying on his hands was the actual instrument of its being conferred.<div eID="gen37324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37325" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the presbytery--</hi>In <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2Ti 1:6</reference> the apostle mentions only his own laying on of hands. But there his aim is to remind Timothy specially of the part he himself took in imparting to him the gift. Here he mentions the fact, quite consistent with the other, that the neighboring presbyters took part in the ordination or consecration, he, however, taking the foremost part. Paul, though having the general oversight of the elders everywhere, was an elder himself (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.1">1Pe 5:1</reference>; 2Jo 1). As the president of the synagogue, so the bishop of the Church alone could ordain, he acting as the representative, and in the name of the whole presbytery [Vitringa]. So, in the Anglican Church, the bishop ordains, the presbyters or priests present joining with him in laying on hands. <div eID="gen37325" type="x-p"/>
